notes: Crux lead binarizes the debate to two camps (supply restriction vs financialization) — 'banned building or turned them into investments' — leaving the Demand-Side Skeptic's inequality diagnosis out of the headline framing even though its prevalence_weight (45) is close to the Financialization Critic's (60). The empirical crux body does include income growth/inequality, so no reader is misled, but a three-way lead (or folding inequality into the second clause) would better reflect the position set.

The 'Institutional investor share · 2%' basics stat is the only basics entry touching the Financialization camp, and its note/detail lean rebuttal-flavored ('dwarfed by small investors', 'actually retreating') rather than descriptive. The camp's own strongest numbers (25.7% overall investor purchase share, RealPage/Phoenix algorithmic-pricing coverage) appear only in the detail or the position card. Consider a more neutral note phrasing or promoting the 25.7% overall-investor figure to the headline value with the 2% institutional split in the detail — the current framing is accurate and the position card carries the camp's case, so this does not mislead, but it is the one basics entry that reads as arguing with a camp rather than informing.

Basics evidentiary weight skews supply-side (zoning premium, new-building rent effect, Auckland, Ganong-Shoag) with no equivalent headline stat for the Demand-Side Skeptic's core claim (e.g., a superstar-cities price-vs-income divergence figure beyond the OECD index). This mostly reflects the real literature's asymmetry, which the editorial rules permit, but one demand-side-native stat would tighten parity.

Action counts are slightly uneven: Supply Liberalizer and Tenant Decommodifier get two actions each (learn + volunteer), while Financialization Critic, Demand-Side Skeptic, and Georgist get one. Not misleading, but easy to even out.

Question 6's closing phrase 'dressed up in empirical-sounding debates' is mildly dismissive of both sides' empirical framing; a flatter phrasing ('though it is often argued in empirical terms') would keep the same point without the edge.

Georgist and Tenant Decommodifier steelman lines run past the ~90-char banner target (~110 and ~100 chars); the distribution stage can trim, e.g. 'Tax the location, not the home — you can't dodge a tax on land you're sitting on.'

Joseph Gyourko appears as a proponent of both Supply Liberalizer (zoning tax) and Demand-Side Skeptic (superstar cities). Both attributions are accurate to his work, but listing the same economist in opposing camps may confuse readers — consider dropping Gyourko/Mayer/Sinai from the Skeptic proponent list and keeping them only in its detail text as intellectual roots.
Tenant Decommodifier's representative_name contains an HTML entity ('Madden & Marcuse') and names a book/model rather than a person, unlike the other four positions — normalize for consistency.
Financialization Critic's description ends without the 'Sources:' link block that Supply Liberalizer and Georgist have; the claims are sourced in detail/basics, but format parity would be nice.

The localist/homeowner (NIMBY) perspective exists only inside the 'who should decide' question; that placement is defensible since it isn't a cost diagnosis, but worth a conscious editorial confirmation.

blocking.issue: Cost-burdened renters stat is misattributed and one detail is wrong. The figures (22.6M renter households, half of renters, 83% of <$30k renters, ~12.1M severely burdened, 2023 data) come from JCHS's State of the Nation's Housing 2025 — the cited report, America's Rental Housing 2024 (https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/americas-rental-housing-2024), reports 22.4M in 2022. Also, JCHS/NLIHC describe 2023 as the THIRD consecutive record year, not the fourth.
blocking.fix: Change source to JCHS State of the Nation's Housing 2025 (e.g. https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/blog/housing-cost-burdens-climb-record-levels-again-2023 or the SOTN 2025 report page), source_published '2025 (data 2023)'; change 'fourth consecutive record year' to 'third'; use 12.1M for severely burdened.

blocking.issue: Institutional-investor stat is mis-stated on two axes versus its cited source. The CNBC/BatchData article says investors owning 1,000+ properties account for ~2% of investor-OWNED homes (a stock share) and are net sellers; it does not say institutions with '100+ homes' bought 'under 2% of US home sales in 2024' (a purchase-flow share with a different threshold). The 25.7%-of-2024-sales and ~91% small-investor (1-5 props 87% + 6-10 props 4% of investor-owned homes) figures do check out.
blocking.fix: Restate the stat to match the source: 'Investors owning 1,000+ homes hold about 2% of investor-owned homes and have been net sellers', citing CNBC/BatchData — or, if a purchases-share framing is wanted, find and cite a source that actually measures institutional share of purchases (e.g. Realtor.com/Parcl Labs) and use its threshold.

blocking.issue: Zoning-premium stat is misattributed. The city-level shares (SF 50%+, LA ~34%, Boston ~19% of house value as 'zoning tax') are from Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks (2005), 'Why Have Housing Prices Gone Up?' — verified they do NOT appear in the cited 2003 FRBNY paper (I downloaded the PDF; its tables are hedonic land prices and regressions, no per-city zoning-tax-share percentages).
blocking.fix: Point source_url to the 2005 paper, e.g. https://www.hks.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/centers/taubman/files/Glaeser_05_PricesGoneUp.pdf (or the Stanford mirror), source_label 'Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks (AER 2005)', source_published '2005 (1999-2000 data)'.

blocking.issue: Wrong proponent name in the Supply Liberalizer detail: 'their 2005 follow-up with Albert Saks' — the co-author is Raven Saks (Glaeser, Gyourko & Saks).

notes: Verified accurate: Freddie Mac 3.7M shortage (Nov 2024, Q3 2024 data, page live); NLIHC 7.1M gap; Pew 2025 study (1,654 zip codes, 10% supply -> 1.4pts lower rent growth); Auckland upzoning ~28% rent effect and both URLs (Cowles + Auckland EPC PDF) live; Ganong & Shoag 1.8%/yr convergence, NBER PDF live; Buchholz/Kemeny/Randolph/Storper 2026 LSE III working paper exists and is characterized fairly; RealPage DOJ proposed settlement (Nov 24, 2025: 12-month-old data, no real-time competitor data) confirmed; Phoenix 70% figure confirmed (Arizona AG suit); investor 25.7% of 2024 sales confirmed; homeownership 65.6% and 69.2% peak correct; ROAD to Housing Act passed Senate 85-5 / House 358-32 in June 2026 with 350-home institutional purchase restriction — confirmed.

why_now could be sharpened: the Act became law TODAY (July 11, 2026) without the President's signature after passing in June — 'passed overwhelmingly in June 2026' is accurate but the just-became-law fact is stronger and the investor threshold is 350 homes.
RealPage settlement is a PROPOSED consent decree pending court approval, with no admission of wrongdoing — 'agreed to stop' is fine but consider 'agreed in a proposed settlement'.

Phoenix 70% is strictly 'units owned/operated/managed by companies contracted with RealPage' (Arizona AG complaint), slightly broader than 'priced through software using that shared data' — soften a notch.

Supply Liberalizer detail calls the 2002 NBER paper 'Zoning's Steep Price'; the NBER WP (w8835) is titled 'The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability' — 'Zoning's Steep Price' was the Regulation magazine version. Minor title conflation.

Rent-control stat cites Wikipedia; the ~182-jurisdictions figure originates with NMHC/Urban Institute tracking — a primary tracker (e.g. NMHC rent-control map or Urban Institute) would be a stronger citation for a tier-3 stat.

Financialization Critic detail's 'roughly 0.35% of the single-family stock' held by 1,000+ portfolios — most estimates land at ~0.4-0.6% (roughly 450-500k homes); consider 'roughly half a percent' or cite a specific tracker (Urban Institute).
Vienna 44% / Netherlands 30% ranked stat cites the OECD PH4.2 national dataset, which won't contain a Vienna city figure; consider adding a City of Vienna source alongside OECD.

URL health: all 19 source/action URLs are live. JCHS, Pew, OECD indicator page, and FRED return 403/000 to curl due to bot-blocking, but all four pages are confirmed live via search/cache; CNBC, Auckland PDF, OECD PDF, Lincoln Institute, NBER, NY Fed, Upjohn, PESP, Homes Guarantee, Tenant Federation, Groundwork, Local Housing Solutions, and both YIMBY Action pages return 200.

The lead's binary ('banned building' vs 'turned them into investments') maps to the Supply Liberalizer and Financialization/Decommodifier poles but skips the Demand-Side Skeptic diagnosis (inequality and purchasing power), which the draft itself calls 'the foundational disagreement' in question 2. The empirical crux text does fold inequality back in ('before income growth, inequality, and investor demand absorb it'), so readers aren't ultimately misled — but a lead that gestured at all three diagnoses (e.g. '...or expensive because the buyers got richer?') would narrow more faithfully. Note-level, not blocking, since the crux body carries the full disagreement.

Subtitle 'they split on whether scarcity is the cause or the business model' has the same two-camp compression; consider 'whether scarcity, unequal demand, or the business model is the cause' if it fits the register.

The values crux is genuinely a values fork (commodity vs right, plus who decides) with no verdict — good. One small addition that would sharpen it: the Georgist camp's distinctive values claim (land value is community-created and publicly owed) isn't reflected in either crux axis, though at prevalence 25 this is a defensible omission.
No house verdict anywhere in the crux; the empirical paragraph's 'cut one way / cut the other' construction is a good model of honest non-balance rather than 'both sides have a point' filler.

Crux subtitle ('they split on whether scarcity is the cause or the business model') compresses five camps into a two-way split that excludes the Demand-Side Skeptic diagnosis (inequality/purchasing power, neither scarcity-by-ban nor financialization). Not blocking because that camp's steelman ('The crisis is who can pay, not what's allowed to be built') and Q2 sit above the fold and correct the picture — but consider rewording the subtitle to a three-way fork, e.g. '...split on whether the cause is banned building, concentrated purchasing power, or the business model.'

Institutional investor stat: the record 25.7% TOTAL investor share of 2024 purchases lives only in the detail field. The compact note is honest ('under 2%... dwarfed by small investors') and Q3's why presents both readings, but a reader can't gauge the overall investor footprint from the compact layer; consider working the ~26% total into the note if it fits.

Zoning cost premium stat: the detail-only caveats that (a) in most of the US the price/construction-cost gap is small and (b) the underlying data is from 1999 are load-bearing for calibration. The note's 'In supply-constrained metros' scoping mostly covers (a); (b) is visible only if the source_published line ('2003 (1999 data)') renders on the card — worth confirming it does.

Nearby rent change stat: the complication that the cheapest nearby buildings' rents ROSE ~4% is detail-only. Compensated above the fold by Q1's why carrying the skeptic filtering critique, so noted rather than blocking.

Price-to-income stat: the detail-only fact that 33 of 36 countries saw affordability improve in 2023-24 is a meaningful counter-trend, but the note's explicit 'since 2015' window keeps the compact line honest.

Question T1 'Does adding market-rate housing lower rents…' uses the term of art 'filtering' in the compact question text; the adjacent 'why' does define it ('new homes free up older, cheaper ones as movers trade up'), so it clears the bar, but moving the plain gloss into the question text itself (e.g. 'how fast do freed-up older homes reach low-income households') would be cleaner.

Stat 'House price-to-income growth': value/unit reads '31 pts' while the note says 'grown about 31% faster than incomes' — pts vs % is a minor register mismatch a general reader may stumble on; consider aligning the unit with the note's phrasing.
Stat 'Housing unit shortage' detail uses the bare acronym 'NLIHC'; expanded register allows terms of art but asks for definition at first use — spell out National Low Income Housing Coalition once.

Action titles 'YIMBY Action: Legalize Housing' and 'Join a YIMBY Action chapter' carry the acronym YIMBY undefined; it is an organization's proper name so it passes, but nothing in any compact field ever glosses it ('yes in my backyard') — a one-word gloss in one of the two action descriptions would help.

Position steelmen for 'Tenant Decommodifier' ('decommodify it and the market stops deciding who stays') and 'Georgist Land Taxer' lean on movement vocabulary, but each steelman's surrounding clause supplies the plain meaning ('a home is a right, not an asset'; 'tax the location, not the home'), so both clear the compact bar.

Stat 'Zoning cost premium': the compact note largely restates the label ('zoning premiums account for a large share of home prices') plus the SF figure; the note could carry one more retainable anchor (e.g. that in most of the US the premium is near zero), which the detail currently holds alone. Non-blocking since the ranked series carries the numbers.

All 12 stat details and all 7 question details genuinely add mechanism, precision, or sourcing over their compact lines — no restatement cases found. Crux if-empirical/if-values also add over the lead/subtitle.

Basics tier-1 set is well-chosen: one scale stat (cost-burdened renters) plus one headline evidence stat per major camp (shortage + nearby-rent for supply, price-to-income for demand, investor share for financialization, social-housing share for decommodifiers), and the 7th above-fold slot going to the T2 zoning premium is a defensible pick given the crux centers on supply constraints.

Mild camp asymmetry above the fold: four of five positions have their signature stat visible, but the Georgist camp's evidence (Harrisburg split-rate, T2) sits below the fold while three supply-leaning stats (shortage, nearby rent change, zoning premium) show. This is consistent with the camp's low prevalence weight (25) and its T3 question, so it reads as honest non-balance rather than tilt — but if you ever want tighter camp coverage above the fold, swapping Harrisburg for the convergence stat's below-fold slot ordering would be the lever, not a promotion to T1.

Auckland 28% (T2, below fold) is arguably stronger supply evidence than the T1 'nearby rent change' stat — a metro-wide natural experiment vs a two-block hyperlocal effect. Keeping only one filtering stat above the fold is fine; if the fold ever tightens to 6, Auckland vs nearby-rent is worth revisiting since the Supply Liberalizer steelman leads with Auckland.

Questions tier-1 set matches the crux exactly (filtering, supply-vs-demand weight, investors, market-good-vs-right) — the right four. Rent control (T2) is the most publicly salient debate left below the fold, but it is genuinely downstream of the market-good-vs-right question that IS above the fold, so the drop-off is real.
Positions 5/5 above fold with all T1 is correct for a 5-camp topic; no marginal camp is padding the set.

prevalence_basis.name: Supply Liberalizer
prevalence_basis.sketch: Zoning and permitting caps on building are the root cause; legalize more homes and prices fall for everyone through filtering.

prevalence_basis.name: Financialization Critic
prevalence_basis.sketch: Institutional landlords, rent-setting algorithms, and short-term rentals turned homes into assets; curb investor ownership to restore affordability.

prevalence_basis.name: Tenant Decommodifier
prevalence_basis.sketch: Market housing will never serve the bottom; rent regulation, public and social housing, and tenant power are the real fix.

prevalence_basis.name: Demand-Side Skeptic
prevalence_basis.sketch: Income growth and inequality, not regulation, drive price divergence; new market-rate supply won't filter down far or fast enough.

prevalence_basis.name: Georgist Land Taxer
prevalence_basis.sketch: The crisis is a land crisis: tax land values instead of buildings to end speculation and reward construction.
